authority.legal_name: San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA), trading as San Francisco Bay Ferry
authority.geography_type: a large tidal bay ringed by cities, with strong currents at the Golden Gate and the Carquinez Strait and shallow margins

mandate.summary: San Francisco Bay Ferry is the public transit ferry service on San Francisco Bay, run by WETA — the San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation Authority, a California state agency created in 2007. It carried about 3.0 million riders in 2025 across 6 routes and 9 terminals, and doubles as the region's water-based emergency network when bridges and roads are out.
current_priorities: Run the 9-terminal, 6-route public ferry network across San Francisco Bay
Deliver the published fleet expansion — WETA projects growing from 13 to roughly 57 vessels by 2035 with new frequencies and routes

Electrify the fleet — the Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program brings the first battery-electric ferries (150 passengers each) into service from 2027, alongside the Sea Change hydrogen fuel-cell demonstration vessel
Open the committed new terminals — Mission Bay, Treasure Island, Berkeley and Redwood City — and study the longer Carquinez and Delta extensions to Antioch, Hercules and Martinez

policy_targets.vision: WETA Strategic & Short Range Transit Plans; Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program; California clean-transportation goals
policy_targets.decarb_note: WETA's Rapid Electric Emission Free (REEF) program is bringing battery-electric ferries into service from 2027, and the Sea Change — the first commercial hydrogen fuel-cell ferry in the United States — has already operated on the Bay.
policy_targets.relevance: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined passenger-only foiling layer above the Bay Ferry network — fast, frequent, low-wake hops on the busy commute crossings (the Ferry Building to Oakland, Alameda, Richmond and Vallejo) that complement WETA's electrification, plus quiet access to the new and committed landings the big boats can't serve economically.

precedent.headline: San Francisco Bay Ferry carried ~3.0M riders in 2025 across 6 routes and 9 terminals — and is already electrifying with the REEF program and the Sea Change hydrogen demonstrator.
precedent.network: Routes incl. Ferry Building – Oakland/Alameda, Ferry Building – Vallejo/Mare Island, Ferry Building – Richmond, Ferry Building – Harbor Bay, Ferry Building – Alameda Seaplane, and Oakland – South San Francisco; committed expansion to Mission Bay, Treasure Island, Berkeley and Redwood City.
precedent.note: Public ferry service is core transport infrastructure here, not a novelty. Navier adds a fast passenger-only foiling layer on the busy corridors.

interpretation_for_navier: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined passenger-only foiling layer above the Bay Ferry network — fast, frequent, low-wake hops on the busy commute crossings (the Ferry Building to Oakland, Alameda, Richmond and Vallejo) that complement WETA's electrification, plus quiet access to the new and committed landings the big boats can't serve economically.

domestic_network.note: Candidate boarding points with APPROXIMATE anchor coordinates [lng, lat] for Grok to snap to real piers/terminals during seal. Coordinates are anchors, not sealed geometry. Core mirrors the authority's live public stops; new/committed/study stops are flagged.

domestic_pairs.rationale: The flagship East Bay commute crossing — the Ferry Building to Jack London Square, Oakland; a fast passenger-only foiling layer above the busiest route.
Ferry Building to Alameda Main Street — a heavy commute crossing into the Island City.
Ferry Building to Richmond across the central Bay — a long commute crossing where a fast foiling boat cuts the time sharply.
Ferry Building to Vallejo up San Pablo Bay and the Carquinez approach — the longest mainline commute run, ideal for the fast tier.
Ferry Building to Harbor Bay on Bay Farm Island — a dense peninsula commute leg.
Ferry Building to the Alameda Seaplane Lagoon — the newest commute landing on the south Alameda shore.
Ferry Building to South San Francisco (Oyster Point) — the biotech-corridor commute down the western shore.
Ferry Building to the committed Mission Bay landing — a short, very high-frequency hop serving Chase Center and the new waterfront.
Ferry Building to the committed Treasure Island landing — a short central-Bay hop for the growing island community.
Oakland to South San Francisco across the Bay — an east–west cross-Bay commute link.

regional_links.note: WETA's network is entirely domestic within San Francisco Bay and the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta approaches. There are no international legs — the whole proposal is domestic.

routing_hazards.instruction: Every domestic leg must be routed through navigable open water with NO land crossings (interior_land_km == 0). Hand-curated waypoints required wherever a breakwater, barrier, bridge pier, reef, headland, naval/exclusion zone or shallows would otherwise be clipped. Use data-clean/uae_hand_waypoints.json format {from, to, waypoints:[[lng,lat]...]}.

hazards.hazard: Golden Gate & Central Bay currents and swell
hazards.detail: The Golden Gate runs strong reversing tidal currents and ocean swell at the mouth; hand-waypoint the marked channels and manage set and chop on the central-Bay crossings.

San Francisco Bay carries deep-draft commercial traffic to the Port of Oakland and the refineries under Coast Guard Vessel Traffic Service; respect the traffic-separation scheme and cross lanes at right angles.
The Bay Bridge, Richmond–San Rafael and San Mateo–Hayward bridges have pier fields; route through the marked navigation spans, never across the pier lines.

hazards.hazard: Shallow South Bay & San Bruno Shoal
hazards.detail: The South Bay approaches to South San Francisco and Redwood City are shoal; hand-waypoint the dredged channels and account for tide height.
The Vallejo and Mare Island legs run up San Pablo Bay into the Carquinez Strait, which runs a strong tidal current; route the marked channel.
Summer fog reduces visibility across the central Bay; strict low-wake operation is required near the marinas, the Ferry Building basin and the estuary terminals.
